quote: One part “Apollo 13,” one part “Gravity,” Alex Parkinson’s “Last Breath” recounts these events, a gripping and at times terrifying account that puts us in the shoes of the divers.
Last Breath wants to relay a remarkable human story in the face of insurmountable odds, but it gets so tangled in its big-picture storytelling and technical details that it forgets to inject life.
[T]he whole exercise reveals itself to be one of hollow dramatic re-creation.
Last Breath offers moments of surprising contemplation. Life, as it turns out, can be very lonely.

It’s a grounded, edge-of-your-seat drama that, like “Apollo 13,” focuses not on one person’s heroics, but on a large group of smart people working together to try and solve a seemingly unsolvable problem.

Adapting his own hit Netflix documentary of the same name from 2019, director Alex Parkinson offers some fittingly intense genre thrills without ever fully justifying why he needed to return to this deep-sea nightmare.
“Last Breath” is a worthwhile endeavor that rewards our empathy, the kind of rare storytelling that triumphs because it is gratifying and extraordinary without extra padding.
While it doesn’t reach its full potential, it is a thrilling tale by nature and it works wonderfully as a tale of human resilience.
Last Breath is a gritty, grounded thriller that knows how to keep us hooked. A stellar cast and a story told right keep this film afloat.
Lean and gripping, but ultimately shallow with cheesy and on-the-nose dialogue.
I have to say, after Last Breath finished, I sighed a sigh in relief as that was one of the most tense experiences I've ever had in the movie theater.

At its core, its pretty damn effective. The question of if this rescue attempt can work and its depiction is appropriately harrowing, even if the movie is a bit surface level -- forgive the water-related pun -- with its characters.

“Last Breath” feels rushed, stripping the narrative of its emotional core and leaving the audience with little more than a bare-bones thriller, where the outcome is as inevitable as it is underwhelming.
It’s hard to deny the power of Chris’s experience, which previously supported the documentary treatment, and now it works as something a bit more cinematic.
Last Breath is a gripping story that still finds the intimate personal moments amid a perilous life or death ordeal.

While the documentary of the same name might be able to capture the more human elements better than any adaptation could, the technical marvel of this feature film's underwater sequences is well worth diving into.
Parkison and his company made an entertaining film, but what's left at the end is a good time that won't feel as moving as the experience itself, which he has already documented before.
It feels strange to want a movie to be longer, but in the case of “Last Breath” I was both desperate for it to end, for anxiety reasons, and also wanting more.

There may not be a lot going on under the surface, so to speak, but “Last Breath” -- always effectively stressful when it needs to be -- does a fine job of conveying just how miraculous it would be for anyone to survive this ordeal.
A capably directed true-story disaster movie with a cast willing to squeeze themselves inside deep-sea diving suits, it’s helped by the knowledge that everything you’re seeing actually happened.
With only so much to offer as a story, there’s not much else to this feature, but it’s a good enough redoing of a story already captured in doc form.

Between Parkinson's excellent visual storytelling and the entire cast, especially Cole, putting their all into performances that feel realistic, "Last Breath" is proof that keeping things real and simple produces some incredible work.
Though based on a true story, this survivalist drama never comes to life.

The narrative is lacking in nearly every facet in which its [documentary] predecessor succeeded; though the narrative version has access to its real-life counterparts for inspiration, its result is hollow re-creation, both underwritten and overly muscled.
Much like its characters, Last Breath simply goes about getting the job done, without fuss or fanfare. Maybe no higher praise is necessary.

The film is only 93 minutes long, and it’s a compact tale that never strays from its central situation. That’s what’s effective about it. The movie never hypes what it’s showing you, always sticking to the hair-trigger reality it’s about.
Riveting, seamless, at points genuinely shocking, Last Breath exemplifies the possibilities of human collaboration -- a feat that has stuck with me and, yes, took my breath away.

The film doesn't devote enough time to developing familiarity with the characters that would have raised the stakes while their fates were being decided. Never mind. The first half is gripping, even if it’s all eventually anticlimactic.
